﴿By the scatterers, scattering,﴾ refers to the wind, which scatters dust and other things. From this is the words of God Most High: ﴿which the winds scatter﴾ [Al-Kahf: 45]. ﴿Scattering﴾ (dharwan) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

﴿And by those that carry heavy burdens,﴾ refers to the clouds, which carry the rain. ﴿Burdens﴾ (wiqran) means a load, and it is the direct object.

﴿And by those that glide smoothly,﴾ refers to the ships that sail upon the sea. In the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿smoothly﴾ (yusran), it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and its meaning is "with ease."

﴿And by those that distribute the affair,﴾ refers to the angels, who distribute the affairs of the dominion (malakut), including provisions, terms of life, and other things. ﴿The affair﴾ (amran) is the direct object.

It was also said that ﴿those that carry heavy burdens﴾ refers to ships, and it was said that it refers to all carrying animals. It was said that ﴿those that glide smoothly﴾ refers to the clouds, and it was said that it refers to the stars that run. Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil* (commentary) on Surah 51, verses 5–7:

﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true.﴾ This is the response to the oath (*qasam*). The word ﴿you are promised﴾ (*tu'adun*, تُوعَدُونَ) may be from *al-wa'd* (promise) or from *al-wa'id* (threat). The more apparent reading is that it refers to the Resurrection in the Hereafter, which includes both promise and threat. ﴿And indeed the Recompense is surely to occur.﴾ Here *al-din* (الدين) means recompense (*al-jaza'*). It has also been said to mean reckoning (*al-hisab*). ﴿By the sky with its patterned paths.﴾ That is, possessing *al-tara'iq* (paths or layers), like the paths that appear on water when winds blow over it. Likewise *hubuk al-zar'* (حُبُك الزرع, the patterns in a crop) refers to the paths that appear in it. It has been said that *al-hubuk* means the stars. It has also been said that it means the adornment of the sky, and that it means the excellence of its creation. The singular of *al-hubuk* is *hibak* (حِباك) or *habika* (حبيكة).

﴿Indeed, you are in a contradictory saying.﴾ It may be addressed to all people, since they differ: some are believers and some are disbelievers. It may also be addressed to the disbelievers specifically, since they differ: some of them said he is a sorcerer (sāḥir), some said he is a soothsayer (kāhin), and some said he is a poet (shā'ir).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verse 9:

﴿Whoever is turned away from it is turned away.﴾ The meaning of yu'fak (is turned away) is yasrifu (is diverted). The pronoun in ʿanhu (from it/Him) may carry four possible meanings. The first: that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to the Qur'an, or to Islam, and the meaning is: whoever is diverted from belief in it is diverted, that is, whoever was predestined in God's knowledge to be diverted. The second: that the pronoun refers to what you are promised (mā tūʿadūn) or to the religion (al-dīn), and the meaning is: whoever is diverted from belief in it is diverted. The third: that the pronoun refers to the discordant speech (al-qawl al-mukhtalif), and the meaning is: whoever God has decreed for happiness is turned away from that speech toward Islam. This view is good, except that the usage of afaka and yu'fak in common custom is for turning from good to evil, whereas this is turning from evil to good. The fourth: that the pronoun refers to the discordant speech, and ʿan is causal (sababiyya), and the meaning is: by means of that speech, whoever is diverted from belief is diverted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 10–14:

﴿Killed be the conjecturers﴾ It is an invocation against them, like the saying "May God kill you" (qātalaka Allāh). It was said that qutila here means "cursed" (lu'ina). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "The wording does not require that meaning." Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its origin is the invocation of killing, then it came to be used in the sense of cursing and reviling." Al-Kharrasun (the conjecturers) are the liars. The root of kharṣ is guesswork (takhmin), speaking by conjecture. The reference is to the disbelievers. It was said that it refers to the soothsayers (kuhhān), but the first view is more apparent.

﴿Who are in heedlessness, inattentive﴾ Al-ghamrah is that which covers a person's intellect. Its origin is from ghamrat al-ma' (the surge of water), and what is meant here is ignorance and heedlessness toward reflection.

﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Judgment?"﴾ That is, they say: "When is the Day of Judgment?" in a manner of disbelief in its occurrence and mockery.

﴿The Day when they will be tried over the Fire.﴾ This is the answer to their question. The meaning of yuftanūn is: they will be burned and tormented. From this comes the saying that the lava field (al-ḥarrah) is called fatīn, because the sun burned its stones. It is possible that yawmuhum is declinable (muʿrab), and its governing element is an implied one, its estimate being: "that occurs on the Day when they will be tried over the Fire." It is also possible that it is indeclinable (mabnī) because it is attached to an indeclinable word, and on this basis it may be in the position of an accusative governed by the implied verb as we mentioned, or in the position of a nominative, the estimate being: "it is the Day when they will be tried over the Fire."

﴿"Taste your trial."﴾ That is, it will be said to them: "Taste your burning."

ِ﴿Taking what their Lord has given them﴾. Meaning: they will receive in Paradise what their Lord has given them of good things and bliss. Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verse 17:

﴿They used to sleep but little of the night.﴾ Al-huju' means sleep. There are two opinions regarding the meaning of the verse. The first, and it is the correct one, is that they would sleep a little of the night and spend most of the night awake in prayer, supplication and calling upon God. The second is that they would not sleep at all at night, neither a little nor a lot. The grammatical analysis (i'rab) differs according to the two meanings.

As for the first opinion, there are four possible analyses (i'rab). The first: qalilan (little) is the predicate of kanu (they were), and ma yahja'un (what they sleep) is the subject of qalilan, since qalilan is an adjective in the form of the active participle (sifah mushabbahah bi-ism al-fa'il); ma is then a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and the sense is: they were little in their sleeping at night. The second is like this, except that ma is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and the sense is: they were little in that in which they slept of the night. The third: ma is a superfluous particle (za'idah), qalilan is an adverb of time (zarf), and its governing element is yahja'un, and the sense is: they slept for a little time of the night. The fourth is like this, except that qalilan is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf), and the sense is: they slept a little sleep.

As for the second opinion, there are two possible analyses. One: ma is a negation particle, qalilan is an adverb of time, and its governing element is yahja'un, and the sense is: they did not sleep a little of the night. The other: ma is a negation particle, qalilan is the predicate of kana, and the sense is: they were few among the people; then he begins with his saying: ﴿min al-layli ma yahja'un﴾ (of the night, they did not sleep). Both analyses are invalid according to the scholars of Arabic grammar (ahl al-'arabiyyah), because a negation particle (ma) does not govern what precedes it with what follows it. Thus the weakness of this meaning is evident from the invalidity of its grammatical analysis.

﴿And in the pre-dawn hours they would seek forgiveness﴾. That is, they ask God to forgive their sins. The "asḥār" (pre-dawn hours) are the last part of the night. A hadith (a report of the Prophet's sayings and actions) states that God, exalted is He, says in the last third of the night: "Whoever asks Me for forgiveness, I will forgive him." It has also been said that the meaning of "yastaghfirūn" (they seek forgiveness) is "yuṣallūn" (they pray), but this is far from the wording.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verse 19:

﴿And in their wealth there was a right for the one who asks and the deprived.﴾ Al-haqq (the due right) here means voluntary charities (nawafil al-sadaqat). It was said that it refers to zakat, but this is far-fetched, because the verse is Meccan, and zakat was only made obligatory in Medina. It was also said that the verse is abrogated (mansukh) by zakat, but this is unnecessary, because abrogation (naskh) only occurs where there is a contradiction (ta'arud), and there is no contradiction between zakat and voluntary charities. Calling voluntary charities a "right" is like His saying: ﴿a right upon the doers of good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], even though it is not obligatory. Some scholars said: it is a right other than zakat, and Ibn 'Atiyyah preferred this view.

People differed concerning al-mahrum (the deprived), so much so that al-Sha'bi said: "I am unable to know what the deprived (al-mahrum) is." It was said: the deprived is the one who has no share in the public treasury (bayt al-mal). It was said: the one whose produce has been destroyed. It was said: the one whose livestock has died. The common meaning encompassing these is that the deprived is the poor person who conceals his condition.

And in yourselves. This is a pointer to the signs and lessons contained in the creation of man. Some scholars have said about it that in it are five thousand wisdoms, and some of them said: man is an abridged copy of the world.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verse 22:

﴿And in the sky is your provision, and that which you are promised.﴾ Meaning: "And in the sky is your provision" refers to the rain. It is also said: the decree and the divine measure. It is possible that "and that which you are promised" comes from promise and threat, and all of it is in the sky. For this reason it is said: it means Paradise and Hell. It is also said: good and evil.

﴿Indeed, it is the truth﴾. This is the answer to the oath. The pronoun refers either to what preceded of the verses, or to the provision, or to what you are promised. ﴿Just as your speech﴾, meaning it is truth like your speaking, which cannot be doubted. The word "ما" (ma) here is redundant (zā'idah). The word "مثل" (mithl) has been read in two ways. In the nominative (mithlu), it is an adjective (ṣifah) of "حق" (ḥaqq). In the accusative (mithla), it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "حق" (ḥaqq), or of the hidden pronoun within it. It may also be an adjective of "حق" (ḥaqq) that is indeclinable (mabnī) because it is attached (idāfah) to an indeclinable word, or because it is compounded with "ما" (ma), so that it becomes like "أينما" (aynamā) and "كلما" (kullamā).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 24–25:

﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾ The interrogative in such a case is intended to magnify and emphasize the matter. "The guests of Abraham" (ḍayf Ibrāhīm) are the angels who came to give him the good news of a son and to announce the destruction of the people of Lot. They are described as "the honored" (al-mukramīn) because they are honored in the sight of God, and because Abraham, peace be upon him, honored them: he served them himself and hastened to prepare their hospitality. The element governing "when they entered" (idh dakhalū), according to this view, is "the honored" (al-mukramīn). It is also possible that the governing element is something omitted, with the sense: "Remember" (udhkur).

﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ (qālū salāman). The first word is in the accusative because it carries the sense of a request, and it is the object of a verb that is implied: the verb is understood as "We say" or "We wish" (salāman as a direct object of an implied verb). The second word is in the nominative because it is a predicate, with the sense: "My affair is peace" (amrī salām). This is on the understanding that "peace" means safety. If it means a greeting (taḥiyya), then the second word is put in the nominative to indicate the establishment of peace, so that he has greeted them with something more complete than what they greeted him with. On this view the first "salām" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with the sense: "We greet you with a greeting" (sallamnā ʿalayka salāman). The second "salām" begins with the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the sense: "Peace be upon you" (salāmun ʿalaykum), a people unknown (qawmun munkarūn), that is, he did not know them.

It is also possible that the governing element is something omitted, with the sense: "Remember" (udhkur).

﴿They said, "Peace!"﴾ (qālū salāman). The first word is in the accusative because it carries the sense of a request, and it is the object of a verb that is implied: the verb is understood as "We say" or "We wish" (salāman as a direct object of an implied verb). The second word is in the nominative because it is a predicate, with the sense: "My affair is peace" (amrī salām). This is on the understanding that "peace" means safety. If it means a greeting (taḥiyya), then the second word is put in the nominative to indicate the establishment of peace, so that he has greeted them with something more complete than what they greeted him with. On this view the first "salām" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), with the sense: "We greet you with a greeting" (sallamnā ʿalayka salāman). The second "salām" begins with the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the sense: "Peace be upon you" (salāmun ʿalaykum), a people unknown (qawmun munkarūn), that is, he did not know them.

﴿He said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ It is possible that *ألا* (*alā*) is used to urge them to eat (*ḥaḍḍ*, urging or exhortation), or that the *hamza* (*al-hamza*, the interrogative particle) is for denial (*inkār*), having entered upon the negating *لا* (*lā*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verse 29:

﴿In a shout﴾: meaning, a cry. This is her saying: ﴿Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?﴾ [Hud: 72]. It derives from "sarrat al-qalam" (the pen squeaked) and other things when they make a sound. It was also said that the meaning is: in a group of women. ﴿Then she struck her face﴾: meaning, she struck it out of shame before them and in amazement at giving birth while she was an old woman. ﴿And said: an old woman, barren!﴾ Its implied sense is: she said, "I am an old woman, barren; how then shall I give birth?" Or its implied sense is: "Shall an old woman, barren, give birth?"

The pronoun in the genitive refers to the town of Prophet Lut's people, since the context points to it even though it has not been mentioned before. By "the believers" is meant Lut and his family: God commanded them to leave the town so that they would be saved from the punishment that befell its people. He described them as "believers" and "Muslims," because they combined both descriptions; we have already explained the meaning of Islam (islam, submission) and faith (iman) in the commentary on Surat al-Ahzab.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 37–40:

﴿And in Musa (Moses)﴾ is conjoined with His saying ﴿And in the earth are signs for those who are certain﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 20], or with His saying: ﴿And We left in it a sign﴾. ﴿So he turned away with his pillar﴾: the meaning of "tawalla" (turned away) is that he turned away from faith, and "rukn" (pillar) is his authority and power. ﴿And said, "A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾: that is, they said that Musa is a sorcerer or a madman. Here "aw" (or) is for doubt or for division (taqsim). It has also been said that it means "wa" (and), but this is weak and does not fit here. ﴿And he was blameworthy﴾: that is, he did what deserved blame, meaning Pharaoh.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on verses 41–42 of Surah al-Dhariyat (51):

﴿The barren wind⦆ He described it as "barren" (ʿaqim) because there is no blessing in it, neither bringing rain nor fertilizing trees. ﴿Like that which crumbles to dust⦆ That is, what has perished and come to an end. The generality (ʿumum) here is intended as specificity (khusus) in regard to what the wind was permitted to destroy.

And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while." Concerning this there are two opinions. One is that the "while" refers to the three days after they hamstrung the she-camel. The other is that the "while" refers to the period from when Salih (peace be upon him) was sent until the time of their destruction, and according to this, "they rebelled" (fa-ʿataw) is sequenced after their enjoyment; but according to the first view, it is a report of their condition, not sequenced after what precedes it. ﴿So the thunderbolt seized them﴾, meaning the cry that Jibril (peace be upon him) cried out. ﴿While they were looking on﴾, meaning they were witnessing it, because it happened during the daytime.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 47–48:

﴿And the heaven We constructed with strength (bi-ayd)﴾. That is, with power. The accusative of "the heaven" is governed by a verb implied (understood) before it. ﴿And indeed, We are expanding it (lamusi'un)﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first is that its meaning is "We are capable," so it derives from al-wus', which is capacity (al-taqah), and from it comes ﴿upon the wealthy according to his means (al-musi' qadarah)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], meaning the one who is strong in spending. The second is that it means We made the heaven spacious, or We made between it and the earth a space. The third is that We expanded the provisions through the rain of the sky. ﴿So how excellent are the ones who spread out (al-mahidun)﴾. Al-mahid is one who makes a place suitable and level for dwelling (al-muwati larmawdi').

And of everything We created pairs, that you may remember. (Quran 51:49)

Verse "And of everything We created pairs": meaning, two differing kinds, like night and day, black and white, health and sickness, and other such things.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary on this verse reads:

﴿So flee to Allah﴾ — a command to return to Him in repentance and obedience, and in the wording there is a warning and a caution.
﴿Did they charge one another with it?﴾ A rebuke (tawqif) [question] and an expression of astonishment, meaning: they are like people who had enjoined one another to say that.

﴿So turn away from them﴾ is abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a earlier ruling by a later one) by the sword. ﴿Then you are not to be blamed﴾ means: you have indeed conveyed the message, so there is no blame upon you.

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 56–58:

﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ It was said: its meaning is, I created them so that I might command them to worship Me. And it was said: so that they would be humbled before Me, for all of mankind and the jinn are humbled (before Him). ﴿I do not desire any provision from them﴾, meaning, I do not desire that they provide for themselves or for others. ﴿Nor do I desire that they should feed Me﴾, meaning, I do not desire that they feed Me, because I am exalted above eating and above the attributes of created beings, and I am free of need from the worlds. It was said: the meaning is, I do not desire that they feed My servants, and the object was omitted as a figure of speech (majaz). It was said: the meaning is, I do not desire that they benefit Me, because I am free of need of them, and general benefit was expressed by feeding. The first (interpretation) is more evident. ﴿Al-Matin﴾, meaning, the Possessor of Strength, the Mighty.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 51, verses 59–60:

﴿Indeed, for those who wronged, there is a portion (dhunub) like the portion of their companions before them, so let them not ask Me to hasten it.﴾

Wait, I must translate only the given text. Correcting that, here is the faithful translation:

﴿Indeed, for those who did wrong is a share (dhanub)﴾ — "Dhunub" means a share or portion. Here it is meant as a portion of punishment. The root meaning of "dhunub" is the bucket (dalw). By "those who did wrong" are meant the disbelievers of Quraysh, and their predecessors among the disbelievers who came before them. ﴿So woe to those who disbelieved from their day which they are promised﴾ — it may mean the Day of Resurrection or the day of their destruction at Badr. The first is more likely, because of His saying in Surat al-Ma'arij: ﴿That is the day which they were promised﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 44], meaning the Day of Resurrection.
